item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees will face the Minnesota Twins for the second game of their series on Tuesday.
After defeating Minnesota 8-3 last game, New York will be aiming to stay hot for this upcoming matchup.
Yet, before their game against Minnesota, the Yankees have now announced news regarding Austin Wells.
Austin Wells Coming Out of New York Yankees’ Lineup Despite Hot Streak
Wells will surprisingly not be in the Yankees’ lineup for their upcoming game against the Twins. This comes after he was their seventh hitter against the Twins last game.
With Wells not starting for New York, Ali Sanchez will be their catcher for Tuesday’s game.
Here is the Yankees’ full batting order for their game against the Twins, per Underdog MLB: B. Rice DH C. Bellinger LF H. Ramos RF L. García Jr. 1B S. Jones CF G. Lombard Jr. SS A. Volpe 2B A. Sánchez C J. Caballero 3B
Yankees 9/15
B. Rice DH
C. Bellinger LF
H. Ramos RF
L. García Jr. 1B
S. Jones CF
G. Lombard Jr. SS
A. Volpe 2B
A. Sánchez C
J. Caballero 3B
M. Fried SP
— Underdog MLB (@UnderdogMLB) September 15, 2026
Looking at Wells
Wells not starting comes in the middle of him being in a hot streak. He has hit a home run in each of his last two games for the Yankees. Although this is the case, New York is still taking him out of the lineup for Tuesday’s game.
Wells will be looking to keep his hot streak at the plate going once he returns to New York’s lineup. In 115 games this season for New York, he has posted 12 home runs, 30 RBI, and a .180 batting average.
Looking at the Yankees Right Now
The Yankees have an 87-63 record and are 3.5 games behind the first-place Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East.
New York has won seven out of their last 10 games and recently clinched a playoff spot. With this, the vibes are high with New York right now, and they will be looking to finish the season on a high note.
After their series against the Twins, New York will be heading out west to face the Arizona Diamondbacks from Sep. 18 to Sep. 20.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Will Warren did exactly what Yankees fans demand of their struggling starters (and it worked)
item.dc:creator: Adam Weinrib
item.description: The simplest thing to beg for from the couch is for a scuffling pitcher to "make adjustments". It's, of course, not that easy. Pitchers are always seeking an edge. They're always experimenting. If they have a lingering weakness, it's not for lack of trying to solve it. item.content:encoded:
The simplest thing to beg for from the couch is for a scuffling pitcher to "make adjustments". It's, of course, not that easy. Pitchers are always seeking an edge. They're always experimenting. If they have a lingering weakness, it's not for lack of trying to solve it. Sometimes, after years of trying, it's finally time to throw in the towel on a given project — a pitcher who can't retire lefties will never be able to retire lefties, and it's fine to admit defeat. But sometimes, as the data builds and frustration mounts, things finally click.
And, as Yankees No. 5 starter Will Warren has shown us in recent weeks, it's not as simple as making an adjustment. You might have to make a whole pile of them, doing endless work behind the scenes, and then it might just pan out at the exact right time, mid-pennant race and with a grip on a rotation spot loosening.
After pitching the Yankees' postseason clincher on Monday in Minnesota, let down by his defense but otherwise holding steady, Warren made it clear that his behind-the-scenes adjustments helped propel a mentality adjustment, too. "I'm not really worried about what's going to happen after I release the ball, so I'm just throwing it with some more attitude, I guess," Warren told Meredith Marakovits in Monday's postgame about the four-outing span that's changed his reality.
Warren carries an 0.96 ERA in his past three starts (a dominant home tilt against the Red Sox that earned the Yankees the tiebreaker and changed everything, followed by the Rockies and a wet and sloppy game in Minnesota). That's the best three-start stretch of his career, and it also sandwiches a 2 1/3 inning scoreless relief appearance against the Padres in San Diego. That's likely where he winds up in October, a reality he's embraced among so many other changes.
"I'm just going to go out there and get as many outs as I can, whenever that is," he told Marakovits Monday, drenched in champagne.
So what shifted? Warren was the Yankees' worst starting pitcher by default much of the season, but looked no worse than a prototypical No. 5 on a playoff team (aka, still fairly solid). In mid-August, he unveiled a new gyro slider, gripped and thrown differently, which starred in the Boston game and earned national acclaim.
But ... again ... Warren changed so much more than that.
Will Warren's major Yankees changes should translate to playoff bullpen role
It's easy to sit on the sidelines and scream, "Do something!" as a frustrating pitcher loses control of the zone once again and makes himself hittable and predictable. Will Warren did 12 different somethings this summer, and it's turned him from "unworkable" to "viable" to "exceptional" in a matter of weeks.
Trusting Warren in high-leverage bullpen opportunities in October is still one final, lengthy bridge that aggressive fans must cross, but his first unveiling in San Diego went well, and with every start he piles up more data that indicates he finally solved the vexing formula that had previously limited his potential. The new Warren is not succeeding by accident. He flipped the tenor of the Yankees-Red Sox Wild Card race, then proceeded to shut down the Wild Card hopeful Padres in an unfamiliar role. The Rockies' offense is Coors-aided, but still ranks sixth in the game in runs scored.
Warren listened to the noise and tuned seven different levers to get the mix he's comfortable with that works. He should be commended — and his transformation should make it clear to fans just how hard these guys are always working, even when things are not responding. Glad he wasn't traded for Adrian Morejon.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Yankees' George Lombard Jr. Shares the Advice He Received From Derek Jeter

The young shortstop reportedly asked the Hall of Famer about playing for the Yankees and in the majors, among
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees' No. 1 prospect, shortstop George Lombard Jr., recently revealed that he had the chance to get some tips from Derek Jeter earlier this year.
Lombard, MLB Pipeline's No. 13 overall prospect for 2026, met up with Jeter in January, according to The Athletic's Brendan Kuty, months before the 21-year-old even made his Triple-A debut, let alone his first game in the Bronx. The young shortstop reportedly asked the Hall of Famer about playing for the Yankees and in the majors, among other topics. But one suggestion from the 14-time All-Star really stuck with the top prospect: "be a stand-up dude."
"Whether that's in the clubhouse or with the media or the fans, whatever it is. Be authentic and be a good person," Lombard said Jeter told him, according to Kuty. "It goes a long way, doing those little things. Whether that's always being upfront and honest or remembering people's names. Just being an overall good human being. It keeps you grounded and keeps you humble and it allows you to keep doing the stuff on the field and producing on the field and helping out the team wherever you can, while keeping all the unnecessary distractions away."
How has George Lombard Jr.'s first stint in the majors gone so far?
Many New York fans will probably be thrilled to hear that Lombard has already been trying to learn from a Yankees legend like Jeter. So far, though, it hasn't been all smooth sailing for the 21-year-old in the majors.
In his first 32 MLB games, Lombard is hitting .218 (24-for-110) with three home runs and 11 RBIs. The highly touted defender also went through an unexpected streak of six straight games with an error in August. While his defense has looked better lately, the 6-foot-2 shortstop has faced some adversity in his first stint in the big leagues.
The Yankees recently recalled Anthony Volpe to play second base for the first time in the majors after Jazz Chisholm Jr. landed on the injured list. So, New York appears to be sticking with Lombard at shortstop for now. And with the Yankees clinching a playoff spot on Monday, the top prospect should get his first taste of October baseball in the Bronx soon.
Justin Binkowski is a lifelong baseball fan returning to cover the sport he loves after spending nearly a decade writing about video games. Before his time as managing editor at Dot Esports, Binkowski attended King's College in Wilkes-Barre, PA, where he was also a relief pitcher on the school's baseball team. While in college, Binkowski was a media relations intern for the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre RailRiders during the 2014 season.
Follow JBinkk

item.content:encoded:
Luis Garcia Jr. refuses to make things easy on the New York Yankees.
Would he play first base? Would he DH?
Well, sometimes, questions answer themselves, and Garcia's role became more clear once Giancarlo Stanton suffered another setback in his recovery from a calf injury, likely ruling him out for the remainder of the season.
At this point, Garcia is the Yankees' first baseman, and he has done a fantastic job. While he was a terrible defender at second base, Garcia has excelled at first, posting plus three defensive runs saved and two outs above average.
Contrast that with Ben Rice, who owns a minus-8 DRS and minus-6 OAA in 2026, and you'll see why Rice has become the full-time designated hitter.
But what about next year when Stanton does return?
The general expectation is that the Yankees won't just be cutting ties with Stanton this winter. They can buy him out at the end of 2027, but they owe him $25 million next season. Chances are, he will be back.
Stanton proved last year he is still an elite hitter (.944 OPS), and we know just how good he is in October. Plus, he is great in the clubhouse, and that is valuable.
Garcia has proven that he is a keeper. He is slashing .297/.331/.508 with seven home runs since arriving in the Bronx, and he owns an .864 OPS with 30 homers and 91 RBI on the campaign as a whole.
The catch, however, is that Garcia is slated to hit free agency after next season, and if he keeps mashing at this rate, he will be expensive. Will the Yankees re-sign him? Or will they allow him to walk once he hits the open market?
That's where you do have to wonder if New York could float Garcia in trade speculation in a couple of months, especially considering he owns a lifetime .738 OPS. This season could be a bit of an outlier for the lefty slugger.
As you can see, things will get a bit complicated here.
Now, what the Yankees can do is keep Stanton as a bench bat, which might actually be better for his preservation, anyway. He is a right-handed hitter and can spell Rice when a lefty is on the mound, and he would easily be one of the most dangerous reserve hitters in all of baseball.
It's a cushy problem for New York, which barely traded much of anything to acquire Garcia last month and is now reaping the benefits.

item.title: [Fox News] CC Sabathia says Yankees could do a better job helping young players handle the pinstripes: 'Different beast'
item.dc:creator: Scott Thompson

item.content:encoded:
It’s been said many times over a century: earning your pinstripes with the New York Yankees is one of the hardest things to do in baseball.
Just take Anthony Volpe’s rollercoaster career with the ballclub, which has once again become a storyline as they head toward the postseason. Through four seasons, Volpe, a former first-round pick by the Yankees, has been showered with cheers, vitriol and everything in between from the fan base whose expectations will never fall lower than World Series or bust.
This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.
If that’s not hard for a 25-year-old to deal with, Hall of Fame left-hander CC Sabathia was even a bit intimidated by the weight the pinstripes hold when he was a free agent in 2009. He eventually signed on and became a beloved figure in Yankees lore — his No. 52 is set to be retired on Sept. 26 — but he understands it’s not for everybody.
While speaking at his PitCCh In Foundation’s 6th Annual Golf Classic at Alpine Country Club on Monday, Sabathia suggested to OutKick that the Yankees should come up with a way to not coddle those young players from the expectations, but rather help ease their way into it.
"It’s hard to watch, right?" he said when asked about what Volpe has gone through, especially now that he’s hearing cheers again after performing well following his latest call-up. "Because he’s from here, he wants to do well. And I just watched so many young players for the Yankees, whether it’s Gary Sanchez, whether it was Miguel Andujar, whoever it is, you get a label and that’s what it is, which sucks especially for a young player. I feel like the only young player that came in and did well was [Aaron] Judge because he hit 50 homers and everybody was off his back. So, it’s hard to build up equity with the fan base when you’re so young.
"George Lombard [Jr.] just went through the same thing. He had six errors in a row, and you started hearing grumblings and all these different things. So, it’s hard to develop here as a young player and I think the Yankees need to do a better job to insulating these guys and helping them understand what it is to put on the pinstripes. There’s going to be ups and downs, you gotta cancel out the noise and go out and play baseball every single day."
Of course, it’s easier said than done in a New York market where championships, no matter the sport, are expected each time a season begins. But the only way through is forward for players like Volpe, whose ups and downs since reaching the big leagues have kept fans guessing. They see what could be, but consistency hasn’t been there for the highly touted prospect.
"You think about Volpe’s perseverance and determination — what else is he going to do? He’s not going to quit," Sabathia added. "This is what he wanted to do his whole life. He wanted to play baseball his whole life, and he’s been in tough situations. Baseball is a hard game, but I think he’ll be better for sure, whether he’s playing second base, whether he’s playing shortstop in the Bronx or somewhere else.
"Wherever it is, he’s talented enough to play the game. Hopefully he can do some things well and help us down the stretch. Jazz can get healthy, they can platoon. We’ll see what happens. But I’m super excited for his future, not only here but if it’s somewhere else, too."
Sabathia spent 19 years in the major leagues, where expectation was immediate for him as well coming up with the Cleveland Indians in 2001 as a 20-year-old. He felt that pressure there, and even for the half season he played with the Milwaukee Brewers.
But arriving in New York was a different story in 2009. Sabathia and the rest of his star teammates came through, though, winning the World Series that season and giving a franchise synonymous with titles its 27th to extend the MLB record.
Since then, the Yankees haven’t been able to add their 28th, making just one Fall Classic in 2024 before falling to the Los Angeles Dodgers. Sabathia hopes this could be the year the Yankees get back and see it all the way through so his squad isn’t still the last New York team to win it all.
But then again, the pressure is immense to make that happen. It’s already begun as the Yankees clinch yet another postseason berth and the chance to hoist the trophy at the end of the season.
It’s pressure Sabathia feels is found nowhere else in MLB, especially for young players trying to make a name for themselves on one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world.
"This is the only place it happens. If you think about anywhere else, it doesn’t happen anywhere else. You think about what Roman Anthony is going through in Boston. If that was here in New York, it would be leading Sportscenter every single day," Sabathia said.
"It's a different beast when you put on the pinstripes."

item.title: [Fox News] CC Sabathia dice que los Yankees podrían ayudar mejor a los jugadores jóvenes a adaptarse a la camiseta a rayas: «Es otra historia».

item.content:encoded:
Se ha dicho muchas veces a lo largo de un siglo: ganarse la camiseta a rayas de los New York Yankees es una de las cosas más difíciles de conseguir en el béisbol.
Fíjate, por ejemplo, en Anthony la carrera llena de altibajos de Volpe en el equipo, que ha vuelto a ser tema de conversación ahora que se acercan a la postemporada. A lo largo de cuatro temporadas, Volpe, un exjugador elegido en primera ronda por los Yankees, ha recibido tanto vítores como críticas feroces y todo lo que hay entre medias por parte de una afición cuyas expectativas nunca bajarán de «la Serie Mundial o nada».
Esta página puede contener enlaces de afiliados a socios de apuestas deportivas legales. Si te registras o realizas una apuesta, FOX News podría recibir una compensación. Este contenido lo ha creado un equipo que trabaja de forma independiente de la redacción de FOX News.
Si eso ya es difícil de afrontar para alguien de 25 años, al lanzador zurdo del Salón de la Fama CC Sabathia incluso le intimidaba un poco el peso que tienen las rayas cuando era agente libre en 2009. Al final firmó y se convirtió en una figura muy querida en la historia de los Yankees —su dorsal n.º 52 se retirará el 26 de septiembre—, pero entiende que no es algo para todo el mundo.
Durante su intervención el lunes en la 6.ª edición anual del torneo « Golf Classic» de su fundación PitCCh In, celebrado en el Alpine Country Club, Sabathia le comentó a OutKick que los Yankees deberían encontrar una forma de no sobreproteger a esos jugadores jóvenes de las expectativas, sino más bien ayudarles a adaptarse poco a poco a ellas.
«Es duro de ver, ¿verdad?», dijo cuando le preguntaron por lo que ha pasado Volpe, sobre todo ahora que vuelve a oír vítores tras su buen rendimiento tras su última convocatoria. «Como es de aquí, quiere hacerlo bien. Y es que he visto a tantos jugadores jóvenes de los Yankees —ya sea Gary Sánchez, Miguel Andújar o quien sea— que te ponen una etiqueta y ya está, lo cual es un rollo, sobre todo para un jugador joven. Creo que el único jugador joven que llegó y lo hizo bien fue [Aaron] Judge, porque bateó 50 jonrones y todo el mundo dejó de meterse con él. Así que es difícil ganarte el respeto de la afición cuando eres tan joven».
«George Lombard [Jr.] acaba de pasar por lo mismo. Cometió seis errores seguidos y empezaron a oírse quejas y todo tipo de comentarios. Así que es difícil crecer aquí como jugador joven y creo que los Yankees tienen que esforzarse más por proteger a estos chicos y ayudarles a entender lo que significa vestir la camiseta a rayas. Habrá altibajos, tienes que ignorar los rumores y salir a jugar al béisbol todos los días».
Claro que es más fácil decirlo que hacerlo en un mercado como el de Nueva York, donde se esperan títulos, sea cual sea el deporte, cada vez que empieza una temporada. Pero el único camino es seguir adelante para jugadores como Volpe, cuyos altibajos desde que llegó a las grandes ligas han tenido a los aficionados en vilo. Ven lo que podría llegar a ser, pero a este prometedor jugador tan aclamado le ha faltado consistencia.
«Piensa en la perseverancia y la determinación de Volpe: ¿qué otra cosa va a hacer? No va a rendirse», añadió Sabathia. «Esto es lo que ha querido hacer toda su vida. Siempre ha querido jugar al béisbol, y ha pasado por situaciones difíciles. El béisbol es un deporte duro, pero creo que seguro que mejorará, tanto si juega de segunda base como si juega de campocorto en el Bronx o en cualquier otro sitio».
«Sea donde sea, tiene el talento suficiente para jugar. Ojalá pueda destacar en algunas cosas y echarnos una mano en la recta final. Los Jazz pueden recuperar a sus lesionados y hacer rotaciones. Ya veremos qué pasa. Pero estoy superilusionado con su futuro, no solo aquí, sino también si acaba en otro sitio».
Sabathia pasó 19 años en las Grandes Ligas, donde las expectativas sobre él fueron inmediatas desde que debutó con los Cleveland Indians en 2001, con solo 20 años. Sintió esa presión allí, e incluso durante la media temporada que jugó con los Brewers de Milwaukee .
Pero llegar a Nueva York en 2009 fue otra historia. Sin embargo, Sabathia y el resto de sus compañeros estrella estuvieron a la altura: ganaron la Serie Mundial esa temporada y le dieron a una franquicia sinónimo de títulos su 27.º título, ampliando así el récord de la « MLB ».
Desde entonces, los Yankees no han podido sumar su 28.º título, y solo llegaron a una Serie Mundial en 2024, donde cayeron ante los Dodgers de Los ÁngelesLos . Sabathia espera que este sea el año en que los Yankees vuelvan a la carga y lleguen hasta el final, para que su equipo deje de ser el último de Nueva York en ganar el título.
Pero, bueno, la presión para conseguirlo es enorme. Ya ha empezado, ahora que los Yankees se han asegurado otra clasificación para la postemporada y la oportunidad de levantar el trofeo al final de la temporada.
Es una presión que, según Sabathia, no se siente en ningún otro sitio de « MLB », sobre todo para los jugadores jóvenes que intentan hacerse un nombre en una de las franquicias deportivas más emblemáticas del mundo.
«Esto solo pasa aquí. Si piensas en cualquier otro sitio, en ningún otro sitio ocurre. Piensa en lo que está pasando Roman Anthony en Boston. Si eso pasara aquí en Nueva York, sería noticia principal en Sportscenter todos los días», dijo Sabathia.
«Es otra historia cuando te pones el uniforme a rayas».

item.content:encoded:
From 1996 to 2014, Derek Jeter was the New York Yankees' starting shortstop. After the legend retired, the Yankees have shuffled through various shortstops, including Didi Gregorius, Gleyber Torres, Starlin Castro and Anthony Volpe.
Now, 21-year-old George Lombard Jr. is handling the starting shortstop role for New York.
The Athletic's Brendan Kuty recently wrote a fascinating piece about a private breakfast between Jeter and Lombard. I highly recommend reading it.
New York Yankees' George Lombard Jr. Makes Derek Jeter Statement Amid Minnesota Twins Series
Lombard said Jeter is "humble and down to earth." Lombard also said Jeter told him to be a "stand-up dude."
"Whether that's in the clubhouse or with the media or the fans, whatever it is. Be authentic and be a good person. It goes a long way, doing those little things. Whether that's always being upfront and honest or remembering people's names. Just being an overall good human being. It keeps you grounded and keeps you humble and it allows you to keep doing the stuff on the field and producing on the field and helping out the team wherever you can, while keeping all the unnecessary distractions away."
Read More: Inside George Lombard Jr.'s private breakfast with Yankees legend Derek Jeter
MLB Pipeline has Lombard ranked as the No. 13 overall prospect in baseball.
Since being promoted to the majors on Aug. 4, Lombard has slashed .218/.279/.345 with three home runs and 11 RBI over 32 games.
Like HEAVY's content? Be sure to follow us.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — George Lombard Jr. se encontraba en medio de la última celebración de los Yankees el lunes por la noche, con la cerveza chorreándole por la gorra y tras haber dado uno de los golpes más importantes de su joven carrera.
El novato campocorto abrió la octava entrada en el Target Field con un doble ante Andrew Morris, mandando una bola rápida de 98 mph hacia el centro-izquierdo cuando los Yankees iban perdiendo 2-1 ante los Minnesota Twins. A eso le siguieron seis carreras. Aaron Judge conectó el jonrón de tres carreras que sentenció el partido, y Nueva York se llevó la victoria por 8-3, asegurándose así otro viaje a octubre.
Tim Hill se llevó la victoria, Morris cargó con la derrota y John Schreiber se anotó el salvamento. Los Yankees mejoraron su balance a 87-63 y se colocaron a 3,5 partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana.
Los Yankees le han pedido a un novato de 21 años que aprenda a jugar en la posición del cuadro más exigente de la organización en plena lucha por el título. En su debut en las Grandes Ligas, conectó un jonrón y brilló en defensa. Unas semanas más tarde, cometió un error en seis partidos seguidos y sufrió un bajón ofensivo que puso a prueba su capacidad de adaptación.
El lunes volvió a mostrar su otra cara. Lombard se fue con 1 de 4, anotó la carrera del empate y ayudó a encender la remontada que llevó a los Yankees a la postemporada por novena vez en diez temporadas. Ese hit le dejó con un total de 24 de 110, un promedio de .218, con tres jonrones y 11 carreras impulsadas.
Quizá la pregunta más importante para los Yankees sea cómo aprenderá Lombard a lidiar con todo lo que conlleva este puesto antes de que octubre le ponga aún más en el punto de mira.
Esa presión ya es una realidad. Los Yankees ven a Lombard como parte del equipo actual, no solo como una promesa a la que le dan minutos de juego en septiembre, y cada error o cada avance tiene ahora consecuencias en partidos que cuentan.
Una conversación de enero que ahora se ve de otra manera
Meses antes de que Lombard supiera que iba a ser el shortstop titular de los Yankees, se sentó a desayunar en Miami con Derek Jeter.
La cita la organizó un amigo común, según Brendan Kuty, de The Athletic, que dio a conocer los detalles el martes. Lombard se estaba preparando para los entrenamientos de primavera y iba a empezar la temporada en la Doble A.
Kuty destacó el doble del lunes como otra muestra de por qué los Yankees siguen apostando por el potencial de Lombard.
«Fue una demostración de ese talento natural para batear que hace que los Yankees tengan tan buena opinión de Lombard», escribió Kuty.
Pero lo más revelador de la reunión no tuvo mucho que ver con batear. Lombard dijo que la conversación versó sobre la vida con los Yankees, los medios de comunicación, las exigencias fuera del campo y la responsabilidad que conlleva ser una figura tan conocida en Nueva York.
«En Nueva York, el rendimiento en el campo es súper importante», dijo Lombard. «Pero tu carácter y cómo eres como persona son igual de importantes».
Ese mensaje ha cobrado más relevancia de lo que ninguno de los dos jugadores podría haber imaginado en enero.
Una prueba de resistencia de 42 días da un nuevo peso a la lección de Jeter
Solo 42 días separaron el debut de Lombard, el 4 de agosto, del 15 de septiembre. En ese tiempo, 32 partidos de las Grandes Ligas ya han traído consigo ese tipo de altibajos que pueden marcar la diferencia en la temporada de un novato en Nueva York.
Lombard empezó el 2026 en la Doble A, fue subiendo hasta la Triple A y llegó a los Yankees el 4 de agosto. Con 21 años y 63 días, se convirtió en el jugador más joven de los Yankees en ser titular como campocorto desde Jeter, que tenía 20 años y 350 días cuando fue titular en esa posición el 11 de junio de 1995.
Los Yankees no te lo pusieron fácil a Lombard para entrar en la plantilla. Le dieron el puesto de campo corto justo en plena lucha por los playoffs.
Bateó un jonrón en su debut. El 9 de septiembre, conectó el primer grand slam de los Yankees de la temporada y se convirtió en el jugador más joven de los Yankees en batear uno desde Mickey Mantle. El lunes, tras otra racha complicada al bate, conectó el doble que dio inicio a la entrada decisiva en Minnesota.
Su rendimiento irregular sigue formando parte de la evaluación. Al comenzar el lunes, Lombard tenía un promedio de .215, un OPS de .619 y un wRC+ de 73. En defensa ha demostrado la potencia de brazo y el alcance que lo convirtieron en el mejor prospecto de la organización, pero su racha de seis partidos con errores puso de manifiesto lo implacable que puede ser esa posición.
Ahí es donde la comparación con Jeter cobra importancia. Los Yankees están viendo cómo responde Lombard cuando el éxito, el fracaso y la atención llegan casi al mismo tiempo.
Boone ve algo más allá de los consejos sobre béisbol
Aaron Boone vio la decisión de Lombard de acudir a Jeter como una muestra de la curiosidad del novato por la franquicia y por su puesto.
El entrenador le dijo a The Athletic que valora a los jugadores que quieren entender la historia y la importancia de la organización de los Yankees. Lombard no buscó a Jeter solo para que le diera consejos técnicos. Quería saber cómo se las apañaba Jeter en la propia ciudad de Nueva York.
«Me encanta cuando a nuestros jugadores les interesa sentirse parte de la organización», dijo el entrenador de los Yankees. «Hacer algo así e ir a hablar con Derek… son cosas geniales, cuando tus jugadores muestran curiosidad. Mira, no todo el mundo es así. Hay que respetarlo. Pero te encanta cuando los chicos sienten curiosidad, entienden la importancia de esta organización y quieren formar parte importante de ella».
Aun así, Lombard dijo que la reunión con Jeter le pareció diferente. Las preguntas más importantes giraron en torno a cómo lidiar con el revuelo que rodeaba al partido.
El segundo mensaje de Jeter llega con el final de octubre
La relación no se quedó solo en el desayuno.
Jeter volvió al Yankee Stadium el viernes para los actos que conmemoraban el 25.º aniversario del 11 de septiembre. Visitó el vestuario de los Yankees y volvió a encontrarse con Lombard, que ya no era un joven promesa que soñaba con el puesto, sino el novato que lo ocupaba.
Lombard dijo que Jeter se alegró por él y le dio otro mensaje conciso.
«Ha sido un año un poco de locos», dijo Lombard. «Pero él se alegra por mí y me ha dicho que siga a lo mío y que no pierda la concentración».
Los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero Lombard sigue aprendiendo mientras el equipo persigue a Tampa Bay por el título de la división. Su bate aún tiene que mejorar. En defensa, puede pasar de estar impecable a cometer errores costosos.
Jeter no puede hacer esos ajustes por él. Lo que le ofreció a Lombard fue un marco de referencia para desenvolverse en esa posición mientras los va haciendo.
Para los Yankees, eso puede ser tan importante como cualquier cambio en el swing que el novato haga antes de octubre.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — With Aaron Judge back in the fold, Ben Rice no longer has the onus on him to be the Yankees leading man.
Instead, he has just become their leadoff man, and a dangerous-looking one at that.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
Rice has spent the last few weeks looking more like the hitter that did his best Judge impression in the early part of the season, just in time for the stretch run and what the Yankees hope is into the postseason.
After going 2-for-3 with a walk — including the go-ahead two-run base hit in the eighth inning — in the Yankees’ series-opening 8-3 win over the Twins, Rice has reached base multiple times in 16 of his last 23 games (since Aug. 19), batting .333 with 14 RBIs during that stretch, including home runs in three of his last nine games.
Along the way — Aug. 31 to be exact — Rice took over for Trent Grisham as the regular leadoff hitter against righties, a role he looks primed to remain in heading toward October as a strong threat to get on base and add some slug while he’s at it.
“I think he went through a stretch there where he really started squaring a lot of balls up,” manager Aaron Boone said before Monday’s game. “And then on the heels of that, the walks started coming into play, where I feel like he’s doing a really good job of controlling the strike zone, which he typically does. But he goes through some stretches and has this year where that hasn’t been the case. But I feel like right now, he’s doing a really good job of controlling the zone and there’s obviously always that threat of slug in there.
“Feel like Benny’s in a good spot right now, hopefully at just the right time to be at his best.”
Rice homered in back-to-back games over the weekend against the Mets — one of them a leadoff blast Sunday — to give him 38 on the year, pulling him into a tie with Astros slugger and AL MVP favorite Yordan Alvarez for the second most in the American League, trailing only Rays star Junior Caminero.
That kind of impact has been critical for the Yankees during a season in which they were without Judge for three-plus months, even if Rice cooled off some while he was out.
After Judge played his last game May 31 before going for tests that revealed a broken rib, Rice was batting .306 with a 1.056 OPS and 17 home runs across 54 games. During his next 66 games, the first baseman/DH hit .204 with a .727 OPS and 16 home runs — a stretch that could have been worse if not for a mostly strong July — as Rice appeared to be getting pitched tougher without teams having to worry about Judge hitting in front of or behind him.
But around mid-August, Rice began to catch fire again, which along with Grisham’s struggles bumped him back into the leadoff spot, where he has spent stretches over the last three years (10 times in 2024, 21 in 2025 and Monday marking his 25th time there in 2026).
“I love it,” Judge said. “Great at-bats, he can pop a homer like he did [Sunday] to start off the game for us, or he’s going to give you a 9-, 10-pitch at-bat. When he’s leading off like that, I want him getting the most at-bats. It’s just fun to see him develop this whole year, going from being a 4-hitter, 3-hitter, 2-hitter, leadoff guy for us. … I love having him hit in front of me.”
If the Yankees can get Judge and Rice clicking at the right time heading into the playoffs — along with Cody Bellinger and Luis García Jr. bringing the more contact-oriented approach with thump in the top half of the lineup — it will give them a formidable top four.
“Last year, [Rice] really came of age at this level and established himself as a force, as someone to be reckoned with,” Boone said. “Then this year, I think has ratcheted it up even more and become one of the better hitters in the game. He’s obviously had a great season on balance. I think he’s done a great job of, he’s obviously had some real hot stretches. Had a stretch where he struggled a little bit, but kind of weathered that storm too.”

item.content:encoded:
On Monday night, the New York Yankees are playing the first game of their series with the Minnesota Twins at Target Field.
They most recently won two out of three games against the New York Mets (in the Bronx).
UPDATE: The Yankees won 8-3.
Alex Rodriguez’s Former Yankees Teammate Still A Free Agent
With the season nearly over, it’s worth noting that a former Yankees pitcher (who recently became a free agent) is still available.
Chris Martin was released by the Texas Rangers last month.
MLB.com wrote (on August 8): “Texas Rangers released RHP Chris Martin.”
Martin is in the middle of his 11th season pitching at the MLB level.
He had gone 1-1 with a 9.00 ERA in 16 games for the Rangers this year.
Looking At Martin’s Yankees Stint
Martin (who is 40) was picked in the 21st round of the 2005 MLB Draft.
He spent his rookie year (2014) with the Colorado Rockies.
Ahead of the 2015 season, they traded him to the Yankees.
Martin appeared in 24 games for the Yankees that season.
He went 0-2 with a 5.66 ERA.
During that year, Martin got to be teammates with MLB legends such as Alex Rodriguez, Mark Teixeira and CC Sabathia.
Other Stops For Martin
In addition to the Rangers, Rockies and Yankees, Martin has also spent time with the Atlanta Braves, Boston Red Sox, Chicago Cubs and Los Angeles Dodgers.
The 2021 World Series Champion has gone 19-25 with a 3.53 ERA in 434 career games.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Ben Rice is forcing the Yankees into a big decision
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Ben Rice is sitting on 38 home runs. He is well past the fun little breakout stage and into the part where the Yankees have to make real plans around him after this season. Rice went 2-for-3 with a walk and two RBI in Sunday’s win over Minnesota, pushing his slash line to .263/.359/.529. He has 92 RBI, an .888 OPS, and the kind of left-handed pop every contender spends years looking for. The Yankees do not need to pretend he is finished developing. They do need to stop treating him like a tempor
item.content:encoded:
Ben Rice is sitting on 38 home runs. He is well past the fun little breakout stage and into the part where the Yankees have to make real plans around him after this season.
Rice went 2-for-3 with a walk and two RBI in Sunday’s win over Minnesota, pushing his slash line to .263/.359/.529. He has 92 RBI, an .888 OPS, and the kind of left-handed pop every contender spends years looking for.
The Yankees do not need to pretend he is finished developing. They do need to stop treating him like a temporary answer at first base or designated hitter. There is a difference between having a productive young hitter and having a guy who has started to become part of the plan. Rice is clearly in the second group.
Rice will still have ugly stretches, as every power hitter does, but he has already shown he can carry a lineup for weeks at a time without the usual prospect training wheels.
Ben Rice has become a Yankees cornerstone
Thirty-eight homers change how opposing managers handle late innings and how much patience the front office should have for anyone blocking Rice.
Rice is a real middle-order threat, not a bat who simply fits around Aaron Judge. That matters because the Yankees have had too many recent years where the lineup became one-man theater whenever Judge was not carrying it.
I get why fans are still waiting for the next test. The postseason will be one. Handling more left-handed pitching will be another. He does not need to pass every test in one month to prove he belongs.
The Yankees need to make the next call
The harder part comes after the praise. The Yankees need to build with Rice in mind, not squeeze him into whatever is left over once the older names are handled.
First base, a regular designated hitter role, or a mix of both can work. The Yankees should let the bat dictate the answer while the rest of the roster gets sorted out instead of treating 38 homers like a convenient development.
Rice has given them a young hitter worth planning around. The Yankees would be foolish to make that harder than it needs to be.
More about:New York Yankees

item.title: [Sports Collectors Digest] Type 1 photo with image used for 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle card sells for record $3M
item.dc:creator: Greg Bates
item.description: Artwork Type 1 photo with image used for 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle card sells for record $3M There’s no slowing down the Mickey Mantle market. Now, the original black-and-white photograph with the image used for his first-ever Topps card is joining the million dollar Mantle club. Hunt Auctions announced that it brokere
item.content:encoded:
Artwork
Type 1 photo with image used for 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle card sells for record $3M
There’s no slowing down the Mickey Mantle market.
Top-notch examples of the New York Yankees star’s iconic 1952 Topps card have been selling for seven figures for a number of years. Each graded copy continues to increase in value.
Now, the original black-and-white photograph with the image used for his first-ever Topps card is joining the million dollar Mantle club.
Hunt Auctions announced that it brokered the sale of a rare Mantle Type I photo for $3 million through a private deal. That is an all-time record sale for a PSA-authenticated Type I photograph.
“This is huge for the photo collecting community, because it’s such a big number,” Henry Yee, principal authenticator for PSA Photo Authentication Services, told SCD. “When you talk about any collectible that crosses $1 million, whether it be tickets or magazines, it’s huge. Actually, photos have crossed $1 million but they were private sales.”
Related Content:
The previous record sale for an unsigned Type I original photograph was $843,750 on April 7, 2024 through Heritage Auctions. That was also a Mantle photo, which became the image used for his 1951 Bowman rookie card.
“The 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card remains to date one of the most recognizable American sports and popular culture items of the last 100 years,” said David Hunt, president of Hunt Auctions. “The record-setting price achieved for the related photograph is one of scant few PSA/DNA Type I examples known to exist and is among the most coveted original sports images of any type. This astounding record-setting image further memorializes the elite status of the Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card within the history of American popular culture. We are honored to have facilitated this historic sale, which undoubtedly has established a pricing standard of great significance.”
The Type I Mantle photograph was purchased by Hunt Auctions on behalf of prominent sports memorabilia collector Ron Firman.
“Mickey Mantle was a great player who was universally admired,” said Firman, who became a baseball fan growing up in a New York City suburb. “Our love for sports and its heroes help bring us together in our communities and as a nation, and that’s very important.
“I really want to thank Dave Hunt of Hunt Auctions for his valued assistance in this process and expertise within the market.”
PHOTO CLASSIFICATION
Type I photos, which are first-generation photos that were developed from the original negative within two years of the image being taken, are rare in general. They are also the most valuable and coveted photos by collectors.
PSA has only authenticated three Type I copies of the famous Mantle photograph with the image that Topps ended up using for its 1952 set. Yee has authenticated all three during his tenure at PSA.
In 2005, Yee along with legendary collector Marshall Fogel and Khyber Oser wrote a book titled “A Portrait of Baseball Photography.” The authors created a classification system, labeling photos Type I, II, III or IV, depending on when images were developed.
“Original Type Is are made off of the original negative in a dark room,” Yee said. “It’s as clean as it gets. It’s the most valuable of an image. It’s right off the negative.”
Fogel is a big Type I photograph collector. He knows the importance of this Mantle sale to the entire photography segment of the hobby.
“In a little over 25 years, the value of Type I photos, as evidenced by this sale, have increased exponentially,” Fogel told SCD. “The reason is two-fold: one is the preservation of nostalgia in knowing that this kind of photography, especially the news service photography, is extremely valuable because it’s very limited—including Types II, III and IV. The second is people are starting to realize the importance of the content of these photos. The preservation of our history from the beginning of the early days of baseball in the era of Ty Cobb, Christy Mathewson, Walter Johnson on through the era of Mickey Mantle, Sandy Koufax and Joe DiMaggio. It represents the golden ages of baseball history.”
MANTLE CARD SALES
Prior to this latest sale, the owner of the Type I Mantle photograph wasn’t planning on moving the item.
However, when a PSA 8 example of Mantle’s 1952 Topps card sold for $3.721 million through Heritage Auctions on Aug. 23, that pushed the photograph owner to let go of his prized piece.
The 7-by-9-inch Mantle photograph was taken by a photographer who was either an employee or freelancer—it is not known—for the International News Service (INS). The picture was snapped 75 years ago on March 5, 1951 during a Yankees’ spring training photo shoot.
With Mantle being an almost unknown 19-year-old rookie, having the photographer take his picture was almost an afterthought. However, the image became iconic, and not many original copies of the photograph survived at news services.
“A lot of these photos, they’re valuable simply because they weren’t meant to be collected,” Yee said. “They were basically a byproduct of an industry, and that industry was basically reporting the news of the day. They were made in small quantities. They were sent to various news payrolls of an agency.”
The Mantle Type I photo that just sold was originally discovered in 2012. Legendary Auctions president and COO Doug Allen found the piece in the archives of a regional U.S. newspaper. The back of the photo is plastered with writing. It contains an “International News Photo” stamp, along with stamps from at least five dates that signify the photo was used by the news publication.
After the Type I photo was authenticated and encapsulated by PSA/DNA in 2012, Legendary Auctions sold the photograph for $59,750.
“At the time when this sold for $59,000, that was a massive record price,” Yee said. “At that time, I’m not sure even PSA 8s of Mantle’s Topps rookie card sold for $59,000.
“It kind of mirrors what the PSA 8 goes for, it seems like.”
In November 2019, one of the two other Type I Mantle photographs that exist—stamped on the back with “Newark Sunday News” and with a chipped corner on the upper right—sold for $375,000. Purchased by a private collector, that was a record price at the time.
“This one is probably distinguished by the editorial markings on the middle right side,” said Yee, noting the third Mantle Type I photo is also part of a private collection.
COVETED TYPE 1 PHOTOS
The Mantle photo with the image used for his 1952 Topps card is one of the most coveted Type I photos in the hobby. According to Yee, the holy grail for Type I photos is of Honus Wagner. The shot was taken by Carl Horner in 1902 and later used for his famous 1909-11 T206 card.
Fogel owns the only example of the Wagner photograph. Yee said if that piece was ever sold, it would probably fetch eight figures.
“The Mantle is considered the modern grail, just like it mirrors cards, where you’ve got the Wagner T206 is the pre-war grail and the ’52 Topps Mantle would be the post-war grail,” Yee said.
The Mantle sale not only increases the values for Mantle Type I photos but it benefits every Type I photo across the board.
“With photos, it’s unique in a sense that it’s kind of like art. It’s not really like cards where you have Card Ladder or a VCP,” Yee said. “People that have Mantle cards, they’re going to ask for more now—that I’m certain of. This will definitely bump and will probably even bump the low-end stuff. When people hear of something like this, they think, ‘You know what, maybe I should pick up a Type I Mantle or a Type I Clemente, just to have and ride the wave.’ It’s like that in every segment of the market.”

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] Un Comentarista De Los Twins Arremete Contra Ben Rice, De Los Yankees, Con Acusaciones Sin Fundamento
item.dc:creator: Inna Zeyger
item.description: MINNEAPOLIS — Durante siete entradas, la ofensiva de los Yankees apenas hizo nada contra Minnesota, mientras que los errores defensivos complicaron una noche en la que ya había mucho en juego de cara a octubre. Pero la octava entrada lo cambió todo. George Lombard Jr. abrió el partido con un doble, Ryan McMahon llegó a base y José Caballero empató el partido con un sencillo. Anthony Volpe y Caballero encadenaron un doble robo antes de que Ben Rice conectara un sencillo de dos carreras al centro.
item.content:encoded:
MINNEAPOLIS — Durante siete entradas, la ofensiva de los Yankees apenas hizo nada contra Minnesota, mientras que los errores defensivos complicaron una noche en la que ya había mucho en juego de cara a octubre.
Pero la octava entrada lo cambió todo.
George Lombard Jr. abrió el partido con un doble, Ryan McMahon llegó a base y José Caballero empató el partido con un sencillo. Anthony Volpe y Caballero encadenaron un doble robo antes de que Ben Rice conectara un sencillo de dos carreras al centro. De repente, los Yankees se pusieron por delante 4-2.
Aaron Judge asestó el golpe definitivo. Después de que Cody Bellinger llegara a base, Judge mandó un cutter de A.J. Minter a las gradas del campo izquierdo para un jonrón de tres carreras, el primero para él desde el 24 de mayo. Austin Wells añadió un jonrón solitario en la novena entrada, y los Yankees cerraron la victoria por 8-3, lo que les aseguró su 61.ª clasificación para la postemporada y la novena en las últimas diez temporadas.
Según el marcador oficial, la victoria fue para Tim Hill, la derrota para Andrew Morris y John Schreiber sumó su segundo salvamento. Will Warren encajó dos carreras no ganadas en 5 2/3 entradas. Tras el partido, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 87-63, a 3,5 partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays, líderes de la División Este de la Liga Americana.
Ben Rice acabó con 2 de 3, dos carreras impulsadas y una base por bolas. Judge por fin se desató después de llegar al partido con un registro de 3 de 20 y 11 strikeouts desde que volvió tras una ausencia de 84 partidos por una fractura en la costilla derecha.
La primera carrera de los Yankees llegó con el jonrón de Caballero en la tercera entrada, pero Minnesota se puso por delante en la sexta después de que un error de Ryan McMahon ayudara a alargar la entrada y Emmanuel Rodríguez impulsara dos carreras con un triple. Los Yankees solo habían conseguido dos hits en siete entradas. La victoria de Detroit por 6-5 sobre Toronto aseguró matemáticamente la clasificación de Nueva York para la postemporada durante el partido, pero los Yankees aún así remataron la faena con su 35.ª remontada de la temporada.
Ese contexto fue importante el lunes por la noche.
Pero lo más raro ocurrió después de que los Yankees se pusieran por delante, cuando la retransmisión televisiva de Minnesota pasó de mostrar el jonrón de Judge a enfocar los movimientos de Rice en la segunda base.
La cabina de los Twins pone a Rice bajo la lupa
La retransmisión de Twins.TV volvió a mostrar a Rice durante el turno al bate de Judge y comparó su lenguaje corporal ante los distintos lanzamientos de Minter. Rice pareció hacer un movimiento evidente antes de un cambio de velocidad, pero no lo repitió antes del cutter que Judge conectó para el jonrón de tres carreras.
Eso llevó a los comentaristas a preguntarse si Rice había captado algo de Minter y le estaba pasando información sobre los lanzamientos a Judge.
La retransmisión también reconoció la diferencia clave: no presentó ninguna prueba de que los Yankees utilizaran dispositivos electrónicos, vídeo o cualquier otro sistema prohibido.
Un comentarista de los Twins dijo mientras se mostraba la repetición:
«Solo estamos contando lo que vimos. Por la derecha lanzaba un cambio de velocidad, por la izquierda una bola rápida. Por la derecha nunca se agacha hasta las rodillas. Entonces, ¿había algo ahí? Solo ellos lo saben, pero todo dentro de las reglas del juego».
El equipo de Twins.TV del lunes estaba formado por Corey Provus, Justin Morneau, Trevor Plouffe y Audra Martin. La transcripción disponible no permite identificar con certeza a quién pertenecía la voz que hizo el comentario, así que en este artículo no se atribuye a ningún comentarista en concreto.
Esa última frase es importante. La MLB distingue entre la observación en el campo y el uso prohibido de dispositivos electrónicos o de vídeo para descifrar las señales. Las restricciones sobre el robo de señales mediante dispositivos electrónicos se aclararon y reforzaron en 2017 y 2018. Nada de lo que se mostró el lunes demostró que los Yankees hubieran cruzado esa línea.
El juez hace que cuente cada lanzamiento
La sospecha llamó la atención por lo que pasó después.
Judge había parecido un poco fuera de forma durante gran parte de su primera semana tras el regreso. Había hecho un roletazo que se convirtió en doble play y se había ponchado dos veces antes de que Minter lanzara un cutter por dentro que Judge mandó fuera. Ese jonrón fue el decimoctavo de Judge en la temporada y convirtió una ventaja de dos carreras en un colchón de cinco.
La reacción de Rice dejó claro lo rápido que ese turno al bate cambió el rumbo de la noche.
«¡Madre mía, menuda jugada!», dijo Rice. «Menudo golpe. Uno se podría acostumbrar a ver algo así, sobre todo en esta época del año».
El repunte de Rice en septiembre le da un nuevo matiz
Las estadísticas actualizadas de la temporada hasta el 14 de septiembre muestran que Rice tiene un promedio de bateo de .263, con 38 jonrones, 92 carreras impulsadas, 96 carreras anotadas y un OPS de .888 en 143 partidos.
Un análisis de PinstripesNation de esos resultados partido a partido muestra una racha reciente aún más impresionante. En nueve partidos desde el 4 de septiembre, Rice ha conectado 13 de 31, un promedio de .419, con tres jonrones, cinco carreras impulsadas y siete bases por bolas.
Esa aportación fue clave durante la larga ausencia de Judge. El sencillo de dos carreras de Rice el lunes dio a los Yankees su primera ventaja después de que Minnesota se pusiera 2-1 por delante en la sexta entrada.
No hay pruebas de que los Yankees hayan urdido un plan ilegal
La repetición de la retransmisión creó un momento polémico, pero las pruebas disponibles distan mucho de demostrar que se haya producido un robo ilegal de señales.
No ha habido ningún indicio público de que la MLB esté investigando a Rice, a Judge o a los Yankees por esa jugada. Tampoco hay pruebas de que se utilizara tecnología para descifrar los lanzamientos de Minter.
Aún no se ha aclarado públicamente si los movimientos de Rice fueron señales intencionadas o simplemente el comportamiento habitual de un corredor de bases.
Los Yankees ganaron porque su octava entrada desbordó al bullpen de Minnesota. Caballero empató el partido, Rice conectó el hit que les dio la ventaja y Judge aprovechó un cutter para sumar tres carreras más. Schreiber cerró luego la victoria por 8-3 con una doble jugada que puso fin al partido.
Para los Yankees, el resultado general está asegurado. Vuelven a octubre. No hay nada que se haya hecho público que demuestre que Rice o los Yankees hayan infringido las normas de la MLB.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.content:encoded:
Wells went 1-for-4 with a solo home run against Minnesota in an 8-3 win Monday.
Wells struck out twice over his first three plate appearances but ended on a high note with a solo shot to right field in the ninth inning. The long ball was his second in as many days following an 11-game span without any extra-base hits. Despite the mini power surge, the backstop has also struck out four times across those two games and is batting a meager .074 (2-for-27) across his past nine contests. It's been a tough campaign for Wells, as he's notched an ugly .180/.278/.315 slash line through 115 games.

item.content:encoded:
Caballero went 2-for-4 with a home run, two total runs, two total RBI and a stolen base Monday in an 8-3 victory versus the Twins.
Caballero got the scoring started in the contest with a solo shot to left field in the third inning. He added an RBI single in the eighth and then stole second before subsequently coming around to score on a Ben Rice single. Monday marked the fourth time this season Caballero has stolen a base and homered in the same game. It was a much-needed productive performance by the utility man, as he entered the contest in a 1-for-19 tailspin at the plate. That's one of the factors that has cost Caballero playing time, as he's started just three times across New York's past eight games.

item.content:encoded:
Schreiber earned a save against the Twins on Monday, issuing one walk over 1.1 hitless and scoreless innings. He did not record a strikeout.
Schreiber entered with two outs in the eighth inning after Minnesota put two runners on base while trailing by four runs. He retired the only batter he faced in that frame and returned for the ninth, working around a one-out walk and an error to close out the contest. Schreiber thus notched his first save since joining the Yankees off waivers Aug. 31. The right-hander had a save with the Royals earlier in the campaign, but he's no threat to David Bednar's closing role. Still, he's been excellent so far in his tenure with New York, pitching seven scoreless innings over six outings, giving up just one hit.

item.content:encoded:
Warren allowed two runs (both unearned) on five hits and two walks while striking out six batters over 5.2 innings in a no-decision against Minnesota on Monday.
Warren cruised through five scoreless frames before giving up two runs in the sixth. The right-hander was hurt in that inning by a one-out error and a two-out infield single before yielding a two-run triple. Warren was pulled after that hit and was thus unable to notch a second straight quality start, but this was nonetheless another positive outing for him. Across his past four appearances, he's given up just two earned runs over 21 innings while posting a 21:6 K:BB. Warren has lowered his season ERA to 3.89 during that span, and he's projected to next take the mound in Arizona.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees news: Austin Wells offers bold All-Star rotation take appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees secured their place in the 2026 postseason after the Toronto Blue Jays lost 8-3 to the Detroit Tigers. Following an 8-3 road win against the Minnesota Twins on Monday night, catcher Austin Wells complimented the club's starting rotation who has been a major key to their success.
"They're the best in baseball," Wells remarked.
New York ranks first in terms of starter ERA and fourth in WHIP. Despite dealing with injuries to key arms like Max Fried, Gerrit Cole, and Carlos Rodon at different points in the campaign, individuals like Will Warren and Cam Schlittler have been consistent contributors.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Schlittler has been particularly lethal in his first full big-league season. Across 31 starts, the 25-year-old has gone 14-6 with a sizzling 1.95 ERA. He leads the sport in ERA and is third in terms of WHIP.
Wells has worked closely with the staff as the Yankees' starting catcher and has been an effective defensive force. According to Baseball Savant, he ranks in the 91st percentile in terms of Blocks Above Average and the 93rd percentile in Framing.
The former first-round pick has struggled offensively overall, but has shown pop that could be beneficial. He homered in both the Yankees' Sunday win over the New York Mets and their Monday victory in Minnesota.
The Yankees' rotation is nearly at full strength, and while only time will tell whether or not the team will be able to bring home the franchise's 28th World Series title, it is apparent that Wells is confident that the group has what it takes to make a serious push.

item.title: [Mi Diario] José Caballero pierde minutos con los Yankees: Volpe y Lombard Jr. le quitan protagonismo en la recta final
item.dc:creator: Eric Conte

item.content:encoded:
José “Chema” Caballero ha ido perdiendo protagonismo con los Yankees en los últimos partidos, desplazado por el ascenso de Anthony Volpe y la presencia de George Lombard Jr. en el cuadro neoyorquino. El panameño, que había ganado terreno tras la lesión de Jazz Chisholm Jr., ahora vuelve a la banca en dos partidos consecutivos mientras el equipo busca definir su alineación para la postemporada.
Números de la temporada 2026
En lo que va de esta temporada, “Chema” tiene un promedio de .232 con 13 cuadrangulares, 47 impulsadas, 31 bases robadas, .657 de OPS, .290 de OBP y .367 de SLG. Además suma 46 carreras, 89 hits, 13 dobles, 26 bases por bolas y 103 ponches en 59 juegos disputados con Nueva York.
El infielder de 30 años llegó a los Yankees como agente libre después de una temporada sólida con los Seattle Mariners, donde estableció nuevos récords personales en jonrones y carreras impulsadas. Sin embargo, su rendimiento en el Bronx ha sido irregular, con rachas ofensivas que lo han mantenido en la rotación del equipo pero sin consolidarse como titular indiscutible.
Su desempeño ante los Mets
“Chema” en esta serie del Subway ante los Mets entró como corredor emergente donde anotó una carrera en el primer juego. En el segundo no vio acción y en el tercer encuentro se fue en blanco en dos turnos y recibió una base por bolas. La gran novedad para la afición latinoamericana fue su regreso al lineup abridor en el juego dominical, figurando en el orden al bate ocupando la novena casilla y cubriendo el campo corto.
En el primer juego de la serie, Caballero pegó un incogible en la parte alta del décimo episodio y luego cruzó el home plate mediante un hit de Austin Wells en la victoria de los Yankees por 6-3 sobre los Angelinos de Los Ángeles. Con esa actuación, su promedio de bateo subió a .236.
La batalla por la segunda base
La situación se complicó para Caballero cuando los Yankees llamaron a Anthony Volpe desde Triple-A el 9 de septiembre, después de que el joven infielder dominara en las menores con promedio de .333, ocho jonrones y 14 impulsadas en sus últimos 13 juegos. Volpe produjo un regreso impresionante con tres hits, incluyendo un grand slam durante una sexta entrada de seis carreras, en la victoria de 10-3 sobre los Rockies.
Volpe había sido enviado a Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre el 4 de agosto después de batear .240 con un jonrón y 19 impulsadas en 56 juegos como campocorto antes de ser reemplazado por Lombard. Desde su opción a las menores, Volpe conectó .295 con 10 jonrones y 21 impulsadas en 27 juegos, ganándose otra oportunidad en las mayores.
La lesión de Chisholm abre y cierra puertas
Todo cambió cuando Jazz Chisholm Jr. fue colocado en la lista de lesionados por esguince en el pulgar el 10 de septiembre. El panameño José Caballero sustituyó al jugador en la intermedia para el noveno inning, situación que lo apuntaba para recibir mayor cantidad de turnos y titularidad en la posición durante la ausencia de su compañero.
Sin embargo, el manager Aaron Boone dejó abierta la posibilidad de una batalla por la posición. “Caballero ha estado entrando y saliendo del lineup últimamente”, reconoció el estratega. En agosto, el segunda base jugó en cinco series seguidas sin perderse un solo juego del 18 de agosto al 2 de septiembre. Pero en el último mes, ya había sido sacado de la alineación en un par de partidos.
La competencia se intensifica
El último imparable de Chema fue el pasado miércoles 2 de septiembre contra los Angels en la victoria 6-3 de los Yankees, donde se fue de 4-1 con una anotada y jugando en el campo corto. Desde entonces, ha tenido dificultades para mantener la consistencia ofensiva que el equipo necesita en la recta final de la temporada regular.
Con Volpe de regreso y Lombard Jr. consolidado en el campocorto, los Yankees tienen opciones para el cuadro interior de cara a los playoffs. La decisión final dependerá del rendimiento en los últimos juegos de septiembre y de cómo se recupere Chisholm de su lesión en el pulgar.

item.title: [Empire Sports Media] Austin Wells just complicated the Yankees' catcher decision again

item.description: Austin Wells homered in Sunday’s 2-0 win over the Mets, and it was a big one. In a game where the Yankees only put three hits on the board, his solo shot supplied half the offense. Both things are true, and neither can be ignored because of one clean swing. The Yankees need a catcher they trust when Octobe
item.content:encoded:
Austin Wells homered in Sunday’s 2-0 win over the Mets, and it was a big one. In a game where the Yankees only put three hits on the board, his solo shot supplied half the offense.
The Wells conversation never stays simple for long. He has 11 homers and can still run into a baseball that changes a game. He also entered the day hitting .179 with a .586 OPS over 114 games. Both things are true, and neither can be ignored because of one clean swing.
The Yankees need a catcher they trust when October gets tight. Wells has shown enough pop to keep the door open. The bigger question is whether the rest of his at-bats can get to a place where the club does not have to plan around the empty ones.
Nobody should be rooting against him. A good Wells changes the lineup in a real way, especially because he is a left-handed catcher with power. The power has never been the concern.
Austin Wells gave the Yankees a needed jolt
Sunday was a good reminder of why he is still here. He did not need a three-hit game to matter. He got one pitch he could drive and gave Cam Schlittler a lead to protect.
That kind of production plays in October. The Yankees have seen too many playoff innings die because nobody could put a mistake in the seats. Wells can do it.
Yankees cannot call the catcher issue fixed
One homer cannot erase a .179 average, just as a cold week would not erase his power. The Yankees have to decide whether the next few weeks show a hitter who is actually finding a groove or one who remains wildly difficult to predict.
That decision has real consequences. Catcher is not a spot where a contender can shrug and hope the good version shows up in a playoff series. Wells earned himself another loud moment Sunday. Now he needs to stack a few normal, useful nights behind it.

item.title: [roundtable.io] Yankees Have a Ryan McMahon Problem They Might Not Address
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: Will the New York Yankees replace Ryan McMahon at third base this offseason? The results have not been what Yankees fans were expecting. item.content:encoded:
Will the New York Yankees replace Ryan McMahon at third base this offseason?
The results have not been what Yankees fans were expecting.
Since arriving in the Bronx in July 2025, McMahon is slashing just .211/.290/.346 with 14 home runs and 52 RBI over 522 plate appearances.
This season, he owns a .212/.280/.353 slash line with 10 homers and 34 RBI across 337 trips to the dish, and while McMahon does seem to have an odd knack for getting big hits, his offensive production has been generally unacceptable at the hot corner.
New York was willing to look past that because of his defense, as McMahon posted 10 defensive runs saved and seven outs above average at third base last year. He also regularly posted similar numbers during his time with the Colorado Rockies.
While McMahon has still been wholly solid in the field, a 2026 decline has been evident, as he has posted zero defensive runs saved and three outs above average this season.
Has he been bad at third? Absolutely not. But he has been good enough to justify his $16 million salary while posting a .633 OPS? No.
The problem for the Yankees is that McMahon is under contract for another $16 million next year, which significantly decreases the chances of New York going out and finding an upgrade at the position.
These aren't your dad's Yankees; this is the more financially shrewd, cost-conscious version that initially balked at making any major moves last year due to Marcus Stroman's $18 million salary ... which they eventually ate after releasing him in August 2025.
You can bet that Hal Steinbrenner has every intention of going into 2027 with McMahon as the club's starting third baseman unless Brian Cashman can somehow find a trade for the veteran in which he can offload that money.
McMahon is 31 years old. He'll turn 32 in December. It's entirely possible that the former All-Star is declining, so it's possible that his defensive downturn this season is not a mirage.
Can New York win with McMahon on the roster? Sure. But is it preferable to keep him in a starting role? No.
An alternative solution is fighting a right-handed third baseman who isn't Amed Rosario to man the starting job while keeping McMahon in a reserve role ... but then you are paying $16 million for a pedestrian bench player. That isn't exactly advisable. Especially not for a team that, in recent years, has been trying to cut costs.
And it becomes even less realistic if the MLB does, indeed, institute a salary cap for 2027.
Is it possible the Yankees can trade McMahon? I guess, but good luck finding a team willing to take on the final year of his contract. New York would likely have to absorb some of that $16 million salary, and I'm just not sure how amenable Steinbrenner would be to doing that.
You would think if it meant upgrading the team for just a little bit of extra case, the Yankees would do it. I mean, they're the Yankees, right? But those Evil Empire days appear to be long gone.
The most probable scenario is New York opening up 2027 with McMahon as its starting third baseman, and while it could be worse, it could also be a lot better.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees ace Cam Schlittler added to his American League Cy Young case Sunday afternoon at Yankee Stadium, throwing six shutout innings against the crosstown rival Mets (NYY 2, NYM 0). Schlittler struck out eight and allowed one hit. He is tied with Jacob Misiorowski with a 1.95 ERA, lowest among qualified pitchers, and also with 6.0 WAR, best among all pitchers.
"I think valuable is a good word. He might be the MVP, too," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said after Sunday's game (via MLB.com). "He's been awesome. Just an awesome season and hopefully there's a lot left in the tank."
The is between Schlittler and Dylan Cease, with Parker Messick and Drew Rasmussen trying to nudge their way in as the third finalist. The AL MVP race is more wide open. Yordan Alvarez has hit an un-MVP-like .238/.375/.393 over the last calendar month and his Triple Crown chances are fading, opening the door for Schlittler and others.
Here are the AL WAR leaderboards entering play Monday:
| FanGraphs WAR | Baseball Reference WAR |
|---|---|
| 1. Bobby Witt Jr.: 6.4 | 1. Cam Schlittler: 7.1 |
| 2. Cam Schlittler: 6.0 | 2. Bobby Witt Jr.: 6.3 |
| 3. Yordan Alvarez: 5.8 | 3. Kevin McGonigle: 6.3 |
| 4. Dylan Cease: 5.6 | 4. Dylan Cease: 6.0 |
| 5. Kevin McGonigle: 5.0 | 5. Yordan Alvarez: 5.8 |
McGonigle and Witt play for teams that will miss the postseason, something that has historically hurt players in the MVP voting. As good as Cease has been -- he held the Orioles to one run in five innings Sunday -- he's not having a transcendant "pitcher who deserves to win MVP" season. Schlittler may not be either! He's more in that conversation than Cease though.
One player not on either WAR leaderboard who will factor into the AL MVP race: Rays third baseman Junior Caminero. He's just out of frame (sixth in FanGraphs WAR and eighth in Baseball Reference WAR), but he leads the American League with 40 homers, and he is the best player on the league's best team. That always equals MVP support.
Schlittler has a strong statistical MVP case and probably the best case narratively. He has been the rock in New York's rotation while Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodón all missed time with the injury. Also, Aaron Judge missed three months with a broken rib, putting even more pressure on Schlittler (and the team's other pitchers), and he delivered every which way.
Judge, a three-time MVP, wasn't as supportive of Schlittler's MVP candidacy as Boone -- "He's definitely pitching like an MVP, but they've got a Cy Young Award for a reason: best pitcher in the game. He's got my vote, definitely, for the Cy Young," Judge said (via MLB.com).
It's not up to Judge -- or Boone, for that matter. It's up to the MVP voters and Schlittler is at least giving them something to think about.
No pitcher has been named MVP since Clayton Kershaw in 2014. Justin Verlander was the AL's last MVP pitcher in 2011. Kershaw and Verlander both doubled up and won MVP and Cy Young in those seasons. No other pitchers have won MVP since 1992.
Sunday's win improved the Yankees to 86-63. They are four games behind the Rays in the AL East and 4 ½ games up on the Red Sox for the top wild-card spot. New York's magic number is one. They'll clinch a postseason berth with their next win or the Blue Jays' next loss.
